questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. The base is clean and indurated. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, non-tender, and rubbery. Dark-field microscopy of exudate shows motile spirochetes. Which statement about treatment is correct?
opts: Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days is the drug of choice
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose is the drug of choice
Azithromycin 2 g single oral dose is preferred over penicillin
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose is equivalent to benzathine penicillin
questions.exp: Primary syphilis is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin has been associated with treatment failures due to resistance.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome on the left side. She has severe burning pain. Post-herpetic neuralgia is most likely to occur in patients who:
opts: Have involvement of ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is more common in elderly patients, those with ophthalmic zoster (herpes zoster ophthalmicus), severe prodromal pain, and immunocompromised individuals. Ophthalmic division involvement is a recognized risk factor.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with black eschar over his nose and palate with periorbital swelling. CT scan shows destruction of nasal turbinates. Which fungal infection is most likely?
questions.exp: Mucormycosis (Rhizopus species) classically presents as rhinocerebral mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis patients. It causes black eschar due to angioinvasion and tissue necrosis. Treatment is with liposomal amphotericin B and surgical debridement.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT for 18 months develops sudden onset of painful red nodules over both forearms and face with fever, joint pains and nerve tenderness. Lepra bacilli count in slit skin smear is 4+. What is this reaction?
questions.exp: Type 2 lepra reaction (ENL) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It presents with painful erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction. Treatment is with thalidomide or prednisolone.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with photosensitive rash on the face in a butterfly distribution, oral ulcers, and joint pains for 3 months. ANA is 1:640 (speckled pattern), anti-dsDNA antibody is positive. Which antibody is most specific for renal involvement in this condition?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are most closely correlated with disease activity and renal involvement (lupus nephritis) in SLE. Titers fluctuate with disease activity. Anti-Sm is most specific for SLE diagnosis but doesn't correlate with renal disease.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with tense bullae on the abdomen and extremities. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigen is located in the:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230, which are components of hemidesmosomes. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at DEJ. The bullae are subepidermal and tense, unlike the flaccid bullae of pemphigus.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with scaly plaques over the scalp, elbows, and knees with pitting of nails. Histopathology shows Munro's microabscesses and elongation of rete ridges. Which cytokine pathway is primarily targeted by biologic agents in this disease?
questions.exp: Psoriasis pathogenesis involves the IL-23/IL-17 axis. Th17 cells produce IL-17A, which drives keratinocyte proliferation and inflammation. Biologics like secukinumab (anti-IL-17A), ixekizumab (anti-IL-17A), and guselkumab (anti-IL-23) target this pathway.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 50 cells/μL) presents with painless white plaques on the lateral border of the tongue that cannot be scraped off. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Oral hairy leukoplakia is caused by EBV replication in immunosuppressed patients (especially HIV). It presents as white corrugated plaques on the lateral tongue that cannot be scraped off, unlike candidiasis. It is not premalignant and usually requires no treatment.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman develops a pearly translucent papule with telangiectasias on the nose that has been slowly enlarging over 2 years. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels. What is the most appropriate treatment for this lesion?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma on the nose (high-risk area, H-zone) is best treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, which offers the highest cure rate and maximal tissue conservation. Imiquimod is for superficial BCC only. Mohs is gold standard for periorbital, nasal, and auricular BCC.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of urticarial wheals for 8 weeks. No triggering factor is identified. C4 levels are low. What does this finding suggest?
questions.exp: Low C4 levels (along with low C1-inhibitor) are characteristic of hereditary angioedema (HAE), caused by C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency. HAE presents with recurrent non-pitting edema of skin, GI tract, and upper airway. Treatment includes C1-INH concentrate and icatibant.

questions.q: A 45-year-old construction worker presents with a chronic ulcer on the dorsum of the foot. Culture grows Sporothrix schenckii. Which topical/oral therapy is most appropriate?
opts: Oral fluconazole 200 mg daily for 3 months
Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 4 weeks
questions.exp: Cutaneous sporotrichosis is classically treated with SSKI (saturated solution of potassium iodide). Itraconazole is now preferred for lymphocutaneous form. SSKI is cheap and effective for fixed cutaneous type. Fluconazole has poor activity against Sporothrix.

questions.q: A neonate develops blistering within hours of birth. Nikolsky sign is positive. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. The toxin responsible acts by cleaving:
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins (ETs) A and B produced by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. These toxins are serine proteases that specifically cleave desmoglein 1, the same target as in pemphigus foliaceus, causing superficial epidermal splitting.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from Bihar presents with progressive thickening of the skin, loss of eyebrows, leonine facies, and bilateral symmetric glove-and-stocking anaesthesia. Slit skin smear shows 5+ bacilli. The type of immunity defect in this patient is:
opts: Polyclonal B cell activation with high antibody titers
Specific deficiency of cell-mediated immunity against M. leprae
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) results from a specific inability to mount cell-mediated immunity (CMI) against M. leprae antigens. Th2 response predominates over Th1. Despite high bacterial load, humoral immunity is intact (high antibody titers). General immune function against other pathogens is normal.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active man presents with multiple painless genital warts. PCR confirms HPV type 6. He asks about risk of malignant transformation. The correct counseling is:
opts: HPV 6 is a high-risk type with 30% malignant transformation rate
HPV 6 is a low-risk type rarely associated with malignancy
All genital warts require treatment to prevent cervical cancer
HPV 6 vaccine is now available for treatment of active lesions
questions.exp: HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types that cause condylomata acuminata (genital warts) but have very low malignant potential. High-risk types (16, 18, 31, 33) are associated with anogenital carcinomas. Treatment is for cosmetic and transmission reduction purposes, not cancer prevention per se.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy fingers, and dysphagia for 2 years. Skin biopsy shows homogenization of collagen in the dermis. ANA shows anticentromere pattern. This patient most likely has:
questions.exp: Anticentromere antibodies are strongly associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-crusted lesions around the nose and mouth that developed after a minor abrasion. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. The most common causative organism is:
questions.exp: Impetigo in children is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus), though S. aureus is increasingly common. Bullous impetigo is caused exclusively by S. aureus (phage type 71). Non-bullous honey-crusted impetigo is predominantly streptococcal.

questions.q: During a patch test, a patient shows a 2+ reaction at 48 and 96 hours to nickel sulfate. What type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis, demonstrated by patch testing, is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes (specifically CD8+ and CD4+ T cells). The reaction peaks at 48-96 hours. Patch test is the gold standard for diagnosing contact allergens.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with recurrent oral ulcers (3+ episodes/year), genital ulcers, and hypopyon uveitis. Pathergy test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease (International Study Group criteria) requires recurrent oral ulcers plus two of: genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye involvement, or positive pathergy test. HLA-B51 is strongly associated. It is a systemic vasculitis affecting vessels of all sizes. Pathergy reaction is positive in Turkish/Asian patients.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with violaceous flat-topped papules on the flexor aspects of wrists and forearms with Wickham's striae. Oral mucosa shows white lacy pattern. Histopathology would show:
opts: Acanthosis with neutrophilic infiltrate and Munro's microabscesses
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ with saw-tooth rete ridges
questions.exp: Lichen planus histopathology shows: orthokeratosis, hypergranulosis (wedge-shaped), irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate at the DEJ (liquefaction degeneration of basal layer), and colloid (Civatte) bodies. These features are characteristic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman develops hyperpigmented macules over the cheeks and forehead that worsen in summer. She is on oral contraceptive pills. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Melasma treatment: Sun protection is mandatory. First-line is hydroquinone (2-4%), but triple combination cream (Kligman's modified formula: hydroquinone + tretinoin + mild corticosteroid) is most effective and FDA-approved. OCPs may be a trigger and should ideally be discontinued.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging pigmented nodule on the sole that developed from a pre-existing pigmented lesion. Dermoscopy shows irregular streaks and regression areas. Histopathology shows Pagetoid spread of atypical melanocytes. Breslow thickness is 3.5 mm. What is the TNM stage?
questions.exp: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) with Breslow thickness >4mm is T4; 3.5mm falls in T3-T4 range. T4b (>4mm with ulceration) with no nodes/metastasis = Stage IIC. Breslow >3mm with no satellite/in-transit lesions or metastasis with possible ulceration would be IIB-IIC. High Breslow thickness with no nodal involvement = Stage IIC.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a 4mm punch biopsy on the lower leg. Which layer should ideally be included for adequate diagnosis of a vasculitic process?
opts: Full thickness skin including superficial subcutaneous fat
Epidermis with dermis to mid-dermis level
questions.exp: For vasculitis and panniculitis, a deep punch biopsy (6-8mm) or incisional biopsy including subcutaneous fat is essential. Vasculitis affects vessels in the deep dermis and subcutis. Superficial biopsies miss the pathology. For leukocytoclastic vasculitis, biopsy within 24-48 hours of lesion onset is ideal.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man on methotrexate 15 mg weekly for psoriasis develops oral ulcers and macrocytic anaemia. Which supplement should have been co-prescribed to prevent this complication?
opts: Folic acid 5 mg weekly (on a non-MTX day)
questions.exp: Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. Folic acid supplementation (5mg/week on a non-MTX day) reduces mucosal side effects, GI toxicity, and hepatotoxicity without reducing efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used for severe toxicity rescue.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful grouped vesicles on the vulva for 4 days. This is her third episode in 2 years. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. For long-term suppressive therapy, what would you prescribe?
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg 5 times daily only during outbreaks
Acyclovir 400 mg twice daily continuously for 1 year
Valacyclovir 500 mg once daily for 5 days during outbreaks only
Famciclovir 125 mg twice daily for 10 days during outbreaks
questions.exp: For recurrent genital herpes (≥6 episodes/year or significant morbidity), daily suppressive therapy with Acyclovir 400 mg BD (or Valacyclovir 500 mg OD) is recommended. This reduces frequency by 70-80% and reduces asymptomatic shedding. Treatment is reassessed annually.

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer from Rajasthan presents with an indurated plaque on the cheek with central clearing and peripheral active border. Biopsy shows granulomas with Langhan's giant cells at the periphery and central caseous necrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous tuberculosis, seen in previously sensitized individuals. It presents as a reddish-brown plaque with 'apple jelly' nodules on diascopy. Histology shows tuberculoid granulomas with caseation. The cheek and nose are common sites. Mantoux test is strongly positive.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with depigmented macules on the dorsum of hands and perigenital area. Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence. The macules coalesce and show convex outer margins. This is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Vitiligo presents as chalk-white (complete depigmentation) macules with convex outer margins (centrifugal spread). Wood's lamp (365nm UV) shows bright white fluorescence due to complete absence of melanin. Pityriasis versicolor shows yellow-green fluorescence. Leprosy patches are hypopigmented, not depigmented, and have sensory loss.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops scaly erythematous patches in the groin and inner thighs. KOH mount shows branching hyphae. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.exp: Tinea cruris (jock itch) in the groin is most commonly caused by Trichophyton rubrum, followed by Epidermophyton floccosum and T. mentagrophytes. KOH mount shows septate branching hyphae. Candidal intertrigo also occurs in the groin but typically shows satellite lesions and budding yeast/pseudohyphae on KOH.

questions.q: A biologic drug targets the p19 subunit of IL-23 without affecting IL-12. This drug would be classified as:
questions.exp: IL-23 is a heterodimer of p19 and p40 subunits; IL-12 shares the p40 subunit. Risankizumab, guselkumab, and tildrakizumab selectively target the p19 subunit, blocking IL-23 without affecting IL-12. Ustekinumab targets the shared p40 subunit, blocking both IL-12 and IL-23.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for discoid lupus erythematosus needs ophthalmological monitoring. At what dose (mg/kg/day) does the risk of retinopathy significantly increase?
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy risk substantially increases at doses >5 mg/kg/day. The AAO recommends using real body weight (not ideal body weight) for dosing calculations, with baseline ophthalmological exam and annual screening after 5 years of use. Recommended dose is ≤5 mg/kg/day.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man develops painful palpable purpura on the lower legs after starting a new medication. He also has arthralgia and haematuria. ANCA is negative. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis. The most likely immune mechanism is:
questions.exp: Drug-induced leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex disease). Drug-antigen complexes deposit in vessel walls, activate complement, attract neutrophils causing 'nuclear dust' (leukocytoclasis) and fibrinoid necrosis. Common offending drugs: allopurinol, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, penicillins.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman undergoes fractional CO2 laser resurfacing for acne scars. Post-procedure, she develops hyperpigmentation at 2 weeks. This complication is most likely to occur in which Fitzpatrick skin type?
opts: Type I-II (fair skin, always burns, never tans)
Type IV-VI (brown to black skin, rarely burns, always tans)
It occurs equally in all skin types
It only occurs in type III skin
questions.exp: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) after laser procedures is significantly more common in darker Fitzpatrick skin types (IV-VI). Melanocytes in darker skin are more reactive to any inflammatory stimulus. Pre-treatment with hydroquinone and sun protection, and conservative laser settings, reduce this risk in Indian patients.
